power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We recruited 315 US-based participants through CloudResearch. This sample was determined in accordance with a power analysis performed using the pwr package (version 1.3-0; Champely, 2020) in R (version 4.6.1; R Core Team, 2026). The power analysis indicated that we would need a minimum of 53 participants in each of the three condition levels, for a total of 159, to detect a moderate size effect (Cohen's f = 0.25). To detect a small effect (Cohen's f = 0.10), we would need to recruit 323 participants per level for a total of 969. Due to the limited number of existing studies that looked at the effect of anthropomorphic cues in GenAI on epistemic trust, we took a conservative approach and aimed to target the detection of a small to moderate effect while balancing the overall cost of the study. We aimed to recruit a minimum of 300 participants, 100 in each condition, with the assumption of at most 20% exclusions due to poor data quality and attrition (n = 80, k = 3, Cohen's f = 0.20, α= 0.05, 1 -β≈0.80). With the final sample, the design had 80% power to detect an omnibus effect of Cohen's f = 0.19 and a pairwise difference of Cohen's d = 0.42 (Cohen's d = 0.49 with Bonferroni correction).

This sample was determined in accordance with a power analysis performed using the pwr package (version 1.3-0; Champely, 2020) in R (version 4.6.1; R Core Team, 2026). The power analysis indicated that we would need a minimum of 53 participants in each of the three condition levels, for a total of 159, to detect a moderate size effect (Cohen's f = 0.25). To detect a small effect (Cohen's f = 0.10), we would need to recruit 323 participants per level for a total of 969. Due to the limited number of existing studies that looked at the effect of anthropomorphic cues in GenAI on epistemic trust, we took a conservative approach and aimed to target the detection of a small to moderate effect while balancing the overall cost of the study. We aimed to recruit a minimum of 300 participants, 100 in each condition, with the assumption of at most 20% exclusions due to poor data quality and attrition (n = 80, k = 3, Cohen's f = 0.20, α= 0.05, 1 -β≈0.80). With the final sample, the design had 80% power to detect an omnibus effect of Cohen's f = 0.19 and a pairwise difference of Cohen's d = 0.42 (Cohen's d = 0.49 with Bonferroni correction).

A sample of 202 participants was recruited through SONA at the University of Waterloo in accordance with a power analysis carried out using the pwr package (version 1.3-0; Champely, 2020) in R (version 4.6.1; R Core Team, 2026). Similar to Experiment 1, we targeted a sample large enough to detect a small to moderate effect. The power analysis indicated we would need between n = 64 (Cohen's f = 0.25) and n = 394 (Cohen's f = 0.10) participants in each of the two condition levels. The final recruitment sample size was chosen to balance our desired detection ability and the availability of participants within the sample pool; as preregistered, we planned to recruit 200 participants or to stop on March 21, 2025, whichever came first. Remuneration was 0.5 credits for completing the 30-minute online survey. After data exclusion for quality control, the final sample was 148 participants (ages 18 to 59, Mage = 20.39, SDage = 4.40; 115 females). With 75 and 73 participants in the low and high conditions, the design had 80% power to detect a difference of d = 0.47 between conditions. Most participants used GenAI chatbots at least weekly (74%), and conditions did not differ on any measured characteristic (all ps > .09; Table 1). Because nearly all participants were undergraduate students in a narrow age range, this sample differs from the Experiment 1 sample in age, education, and GenAI experience.

Similar to Experiment 1, we fit a linear mixed-effects model to test for differing effects of the anthropomorphic cue manipulation on author and content trust. This analysis did not reveal a significant interaction between condition and trust type. Specifically, the difference between author and content trust in the high author condition did not differ significantly from that observed in the low author condition (t(146) = 1.30, p = .196). This difference corresponds to about 0.2 standard deviations of the author-minus-content difference, and the design had only about 25% power to detect a difference of that size; the nonsignificant interaction therefore does not show that the manipulation affected author and content trust to a similar extent.

table.text: The two experiments also differed in population (online adults versus undergraduate students), and Experiment 2 was underpowered for the comparison between author and content trust; roughly 300 participants per condition would be needed to detect a difference of the size we observed with 80% power. Experiment 1 was not preregistered, several analyses in both experiments were exploratory, and the equivalence bounds were chosen after data collection.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.expanded: The high and low conditions produced statistically equivalent content trust at a bound of ±0.30 SD (d = 0.01, 90% CI [-0.24, 0.26], TOST p = .027), but not at ±0.20 (Appendix B); because these two conditions also did not differ in anthropomorphism ratings, this does not show that a successful anthropomorphism manipulation would leave content trust unchanged.
The content trust effect was not significant in four of the five specifications but was significant after covariate adjustment (B = 0.30, p = .008).

Most of this change came from adjusting for how often participants consumed media similar to the blog post, which was imbalanced across conditions (Section 4.1.1); adjusting for that variable alone gave B = 0.29, p = .012, whereas adjusting for all other covariates without it gave B = 0.21, p = .064.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps > .22", "ps > .99", "ps > .27", 
"ps > .09", "ps > .55", "p < .05", "p ≥.05", "p ≥.05"), Text = c("Conditions did not differ in age, sex, education, or frequency of GenAI use (Kruskal-Wallis tests, all ps > .22; Table 1).", 
"The human author was rated higher than both GenAI authors on each (ds from 0.65 to 0.82, all ps < .001), and the two GenAI authors did not differ (|d|s ≤0.11, ps > .99).", 
"Across all specifications, the low and high conditions never differed on author trust, content trust, or their difference (all ps > .27).", 
"Most participants used GenAI chatbots at least weekly (74%), and conditions did not differ on any measured characteristic (all ps > .09; Table 1).", 
"Participants asked about the post, Velocerin, or the underlying study in 98 of 148 conversations (66%), and the chatbot mentioned Velocerin in 114 (77%), with no difference between conditions (ps > .55).", 
"TOST p values for content trust at each equivalence bound (in SD units); p < .05 indicates statistical equivalence within that bound.", 
"Asterisks denote statistical significance: p < .0001 (****); p ≥.05 (ns).", 
"Asterisks denote statistical significance: p < .01 (**); p ≥.05 (ns)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -8L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

stat_p_nonsig.report:
Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 7 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

table.text: There was a significant main effect of the anthropomorphic cue manipulation on anthropomorphism as measured by the Godspeed instrument (F(2, 267) = 85.55, MSE = 0.54, p < .001, ω2 = .39).
table.eta_coherence_note: Effect size reported but not verifiable from F and degrees of freedom alone.

table.text: Upon further analysis with pairwise Bonferroni-corrected Welch's t-tests, there was a significant difference between the anthropomorphism scores in the low (n = 87, M = -0.40, SD = 0.80) and human (n = 91, M = 0.82, SD = 0.54) conditions (t(149.09) = 11.87, p < .001, d = 1.79, 95% confidence interval (CI) [1.45, 2.14]) and the high (n = 92, M = -0.43, SD = 0.83) and human conditions (t(155.65) = 12.14, p < .001, d = 1.79, 95% CI [1.45, 2.13]); however, the effect of the anthropomorphic cue manipulation did not reach significance for anthropomorphism when comparing the high and low conditions (t(176.93) = -0.29, p = 1.000, d = -0.04, 95% CI [-0.34, 0.25]).
table.d_coherence_note: Non-integer df indicates Welch's t-test (unequal variances); sample sizes cannot be determined.

live_data_statements: We recruited 315 US-based participants through CloudResearch.
Participants were compensated with US$2.00 for completing this 15-minute online survey.

Participants were from the United States of America, were recruited from the CloudResearch Approved Participants List, and were required to have an approval rating greater than or equal to 95% and to have completed more than 100 HITs.

Education is the highest level participants reported; most Experiment 2 participants without post-secondary education, all recruited from a university participant pool, reported completed secondary school.
Participants were presented with a brief description and an accompanying image of an author.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three author description conditions.
We removed "Moving rigidly-Moving elegantly" from the anthropomorphism questionnaire because the participants were not interacting with a moving robot.
Participants were asked to rate how well each of these three adjectives described the content on a 5-point scale.
Participants enrolled in the study on the CloudResearch platform and were redirected to a survey hosted on the Qualtrics platform.
Upon starting the study, participants were presented with an information letter and asked to provide their consent to participate in the study.

We indicated that the study was examining perceptions of communicated information and withheld the intention to investigate the relationship between trust, anthropomorphism, and GenAI until participants completed the study.
Upon consent, participants were randomly assigned to one of three author conditions: low (n = 87), high (n = 92), and human (n = 91).

Participants were first presented with an instruction screen that indicated that they should carefully read the blog post and the author's description on the next screen and that they would later be asked to answer questions about the text.
Participants were asked to answer basic comprehension check questions about the content.

On the next screens, participants were shown the following measures in a randomized order: items from the Godspeed Instrument (14 items; Bartneck et al., 2009) and the METI (14 items; Hendriks et al., 2015), which were intermixed in a randomized order; the message credibility scale (3 items; Appelman & Sundar, 2016) combined with the writing quality items, intermixed in a randomized order; and our novel author and content trust scale developed for this experiment.

Participants were then asked about their familiarity with and use of artificial intelligence technology, how often they consumed media similar to the blog post, and demographic information, including age, sex, gender, language fluency, and educational level.
Participants were asked open-ended questions related to anything they found confusing, the purpose of the study, and whether they experienced technical difficulties.
We used the Bot Detection feature provided within the Qualtrics platform to screen for potential bot activity (Qualtrics, 2025); no participants were excluded.foot_0

Additionally, participants were excluded if their completion time for the study was less than one third of the median duration (tmedian = 544 seconds) across participants who completed the survey (n = 2).
Because nearly all participants were undergraduate students in a narrow age range, this sample differs from the Experiment 1 sample in age, education, and GenAI experience.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: low (n = 75) or high (n = 73) anthropomorphic cues.
No participants were excluded as a result of the bot detection check.

And when participants had the chance to interact with the GenAI chatbot, particularly the one in the high condition, they could see evidence that the writing ability was aligned to that necessary to write the blog post.
Summarizing a research study may be seen as an objective task, and in Experiment 1 participants had no opportunity to observe an error.
No participants had a reCAPTCHA score less than 0.5.

text.text: As Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) becomes more sophisticated and widespread, it matters how its perceived humanness affects trust.
Previous work shows that anthropomorphism increases an agent's perceived trustworthiness as an advisor.
We asked whether an author's presentation also affects trust in the information it produces in a non-advisory role.
In two experiments, participants read a science communication blog post attributed to an author with varying anthropomorphic cues.
They rated the trustworthiness of the author (author trust) and the content (content trust).
In Experiment 1 (N = 270), the post was attributed to a GenAI author described with low or high anthropomorphic cues, or to a human expert.
The human author, who also differed in implied professional expertise, received higher author trust than either GenAI author.
This effect was reliably larger than the effect on content trust.
The low-and high-cue GenAI authors did not reliably differ, including in anthropomorphism ratings.
In Experiment 2 (N = 148, preregistered), participants chatted with a GenAI chatbot, presented as the author, that used fewer (low condition) or more (high condition) anthropomorphic cues.
The highcue chatbot was rated more anthropomorphic and received modestly higher author trust.
No reliable content trust effect was detected, and evidence that the two effects differed was inconclusive.
Author and content trust were strongly correlated in both experiments.
These results suggest that cues to an author's humanness may shape trust in the author more than in what it communicates, although the clearest evidence came from comparing human and GenAI authors.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has been around for decades, but with the release of Generative AI (GenAI) systems such as OpenAI's ChatGPT, human-level content creation technology is broadly accessible for the first time (Dale, 2024; Hu, 2023).
text.formatted: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been around for decades, but with the release of Generative AI (GenAI) systems such as OpenAI's ChatGPT, human-level content creation technology is broadly accessible for the first time <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Dale, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Hu, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: With the ease of a conversational message, people can enlist the help of GenAI to perform a wide range of tasks, such as content writing, image generation, or summarizing complex topics.
GenAI is able to create well-formed and believable content that can misinform, either intentionally or due to so-called AI hallucinations (Ji et al., 2023).
text.formatted: GenAI is able to create well-formed and believable content that can misinform, either intentionally or due to so-called AI hallucinations <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Ji et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: As this technology continues to evolve rapidly, it is vital to understand how humans determine the credibility of AI-generated informational content.
In addition to the increasing scope of tasks that AI is taking on, GenAI is becoming more human-like.

There is evidence that anthropomorphism, the attribution of human-like characteristics to non-human agents, increases trust in purpose-built AI agents, such as autonomous vehicles, and trust resiliency when using AI for decision making (De Visser et al., 2016; Waytz et al., 2014).
text.formatted: There is evidence that anthropomorphism, the attribution of human-like characteristics to non-human agents, increases trust in purpose-built AI agents, such as autonomous vehicles, and trust resiliency when using AI for decision making <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(De Visser et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Waytz et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, there is little work directly looking at the link between anthropomorphism and trust in communicated knowledge in a non-advisory situation, known as epistemic trust (Sprecher et al., 2022).
text.formatted: However, there is little work directly looking at the link between anthropomorphism and trust in communicated knowledge in a non-advisory situation, known as epistemic trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Sprecher et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Most of what is known about anthropomorphism and trust comes from static cues, such as a human-like face, name, or description of an agent (Gong, 2008; Waytz et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Most of what is known about anthropomorphism and trust comes from static cues, such as a human-like face, name, or description of an agent <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Gong, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Waytz et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Conversational GenAI conveys humanness differently: through how it behaves during an interaction, for example by responding with warmth or empathy (Araujo, 2018; Liu & Sundar, 2018).
text.formatted: Conversational GenAI conveys humanness differently: through how it behaves during an interaction, for example by responding with warmth or empathy <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Araujo, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Liu & Sundar, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Meanwhile, studies of AI-authored content usually measure the credibility of the content alone (Longoni et al., 2022; Waddell, 2018), so it is not known whether human-like cues affect trust in a GenAI agent and trust in what it says in the same way.
text.formatted: Meanwhile, studies of AI-authored content usually measure the credibility of the content alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Longoni et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Waddell, 2018)</ref>, so it is not known whether human-like cues affect trust in a GenAI agent and trust in what it says in the same way.

text.text: We address these gaps in two experiments that hold a science communication blog post constant and vary only how its author is presented.
Experiment 1 tests static cues: participants read a short description of a GenAI author with low or high anthropomorphic cues, or of a human expert.
Experiment 2 tests behavioral cues: participants converse with a GenAI chatbot, presented as the author, that responds in either a mechanical or an empathetic, emotionally expressive way.
In both, we measure trust in the author and trust in the content separately, and test directly whether author cues affect the two to the same degree.
To contextualize these questions, we first review the technological and psychological background underlying GenAI, anthropomorphism, and epistemic trust.
>Background
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Background</head>

text.text: GenAI models come in many forms.
Some of the most common forms at the time of writing are those that generate text, such as Large Language Models (LLMs).
An LLM is an artificial neural network that has been trained on a large body of textual input, usually via unsupervised learning.
This means that the text is not annotated or marked with groundtruth information to aid in the training process.

Much like a human would read a book and encode the knowledge contained within it in their mind, the LLM transforms the words, synthesizes, and encodes the knowledge into its model according to a particular algorithmic strategy.
For example, OpenAI models, such as ChatGPT, are generative pretrained transformer (GPT) models, which are based on the transformer algorithm (Vaswani et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For example, OpenAI models, such as ChatGPT, are generative pretrained transformer (GPT) models, which are based on the transformer algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Vaswani et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The transformer learns patterns in its training data, and models based on it generate output by predicting the next token-such as a word, letter, or phrase-in a sequence, based on the user input and the data used for training.
As a result, they can produce nonsensical or non-factual output, colloquially known as hallucinations (Ji et al., 2023; Ooi et al., 2025).
text.formatted: As a result, they can produce nonsensical or non-factual output, colloquially known as hallucinations <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Ji et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Ooi et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, models are often fine-tuned after their initial training to make their output more truthful and less harmful, for example through reinforcement learning from human feedback (Ouyang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In addition, models are often fine-tuned after their initial training to make their output more truthful and less harmful, for example through reinforcement learning from human feedback <ref type="bibr">(Ouyang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: There has been a rapid advancement in quality and sophistication of the output of GenAI models to the point that the content is now as good as that of human authors for some tasks.
In fact, recent research has found that the quality of AI-generated content was rated more highly than that of human authors (Zhang & Gosline, 2023).
text.formatted: In fact, recent research has found that the quality of AI-generated content was rated more highly than that of human authors <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Zhang & Gosline, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: With ongoing quality improvements, GenAI has the potential to help us be more efficient and productive in many aspects of society (Ooi et al., 2025).
text.formatted: With ongoing quality improvements, GenAI has the potential to help us be more efficient and productive in many aspects of society <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Ooi et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, its potential to support humans in everyday tasks is conditional on humans' willingness to trust its content (i.e., their epistemic trust).
Epistemic trust is one's willingness to accept and integrate communicated knowledge (Knapen et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Epistemic trust is one's willingness to accept and integrate communicated knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Knapen et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: It is vital for social learning (Csibra & Gergely, 2009).
text.formatted: It is vital for social learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Csibra & Gergely, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: This trust is balanced with epistemic vigilance in deciding what information to believe (Sperber et al., 2010).
text.formatted: This trust is balanced with epistemic vigilance in deciding what information to believe <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Sperber et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: One's epistemic credulity is high when an individual trusts too widely without enough vigilance; in this case, they may be susceptible to misinformation and exploitation (Campbell et al., 2021).
text.formatted: One's epistemic credulity is high when an individual trusts too widely without enough vigilance; in this case, they may be susceptible to misinformation and exploitation <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Campbell et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, epistemic mistrust is high when one is overly vigilant and untrusting of others (Campbell et al., 2021).
text.formatted: On the other hand, epistemic mistrust is high when one is overly vigilant and untrusting of others <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Campbell et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals with high epistemic mistrust may lack the ability to learn effectively from social experiences.
Without social learning, each person would need to experience everything directly (Csibra & Gergely, 2009; Mascaro & Sperber, 2009) and would likely suffer greatly as a result.
text.formatted: Without social learning, each person would need to experience everything directly <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Csibra & Gergely, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Mascaro & Sperber, 2009)</ref> and would likely suffer greatly as a result.

text.text: Imagine the child who does not trust the warnings of a parent to not touch a hot stove because it will hurt, or the parent whose child dies from a preventable childhood illness because they were hesitant to vaccinate according to expert advice.

Similarly, without enough vigilance, one can assimilate false information, possibly leading to false beliefs and taking dangerous actions leading to harm; for example, acting on claims that various diseases such as COVID-19 or cancer can be cured by ingesting chlorine dioxide (Burke et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Similarly, without enough vigilance, one can assimilate false information, possibly leading to false beliefs and taking dangerous actions leading to harm; for example, acting on claims that various diseases such as COVID-19 or cancer can be cured by ingesting chlorine dioxide <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Burke et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: While epistemic trust typically involves judgments about human communicators, emerging technologies introduce non-human agents as potential sources of information.

Understanding how these socially based epistemic judgments may be used when considering content produced by GenAI requires consideration of anthropomorphism (i.e., the perception of human-like qualities in non-human entities).
A powerful social marker that may play a key role in deciding the trustworthiness of an artificial agent is anthropomorphism (Kulms & Kopp, 2019).
text.formatted: A powerful social marker that may play a key role in deciding the trustworthiness of an artificial agent is anthropomorphism <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Kulms & Kopp, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Anthropomorphism is the attribution of human characteristics and mental states (e.g., goals, intentions, emotions) to non-human things, whether they are living or not (Epley et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Anthropomorphism is the attribution of human characteristics and mental states (e.g., goals, intentions, emotions) to non-human things, whether they are living or not <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Epley et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The presence of a human-like face has been found to increase anthropomorphism and mind perception in non-human agents (Broadbent et al., 2013; Epley et al., 2007; Looser & Wheatley, 2010).
text.formatted: The presence of a human-like face has been found to increase anthropomorphism and mind perception in non-human agents <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Broadbent et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Epley et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Looser & Wheatley, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond the presence of human-like physical features, perceiving a mind in an agent can also evoke anthropomorphism (Epley, 2018).
text.formatted: Beyond the presence of human-like physical features, perceiving a mind in an agent can also evoke anthropomorphism <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Epley, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This is particularly relevant with increasing use and availability of conversational GenAI agents, which demonstrate language and reasoning capabilities previously only seen within humans.

Past research has found that mind perception, as well as individual tendencies toward anthropomorphizing, predicts self-reported attitudes toward important everyday concerns: the extent of ethical consideration and respect directed toward an agent; the amount of responsibility and accountability conferred on an agent; the amount of social influence an agent has; and critically, the perceived trustworthiness of an agent (Gray et al., 2011; Gray et al., 2012; Gray & Wegner, 2012; Waytz et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Past research has found that mind perception, as well as individual tendencies toward anthropomorphizing, predicts self-reported attitudes toward important everyday concerns: the extent of ethical consideration and respect directed toward an agent; the amount of responsibility and accountability conferred on an agent; the amount of social influence an agent has; and critically, the perceived trustworthiness of an agent <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Gray et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gray et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Gray & Wegner, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Waytz et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Epistemic trust and anthropomorphism in GenAI have yet to be explored in depth.

In one of very few existing studies, the use of a spoken voice increased both ratings of anthropomorphism and the perceived accuracy of advice, showing a correlation between anthropomorphism and trust in advice given by the GenAI agents (Cohn et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In one of very few existing studies, the use of a spoken voice increased both ratings of anthropomorphism and the perceived accuracy of advice, showing a correlation between anthropomorphism and trust in advice given by the GenAI agents <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Cohn et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, mind perception in GenAI, which is associated with anthropomorphism, has been shown to correlate with trust (self-reported) and with rates of advice taking; while trust was positively correlated with mind perception in general, when mental-state traits were associated with experience (e.g., happiness) rather than intelligence (e.g., planning), attribution was weakly negatively correlated with advice acceptance from an LLM agent (Colombatto et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Additionally, mind perception in GenAI, which is associated with anthropomorphism, has been shown to correlate with trust (self-reported) and with rates of advice taking; while trust was positively correlated with mind perception in general, when mental-state traits were associated with experience (e.g., happiness) rather than intelligence (e.g., planning), attribution was weakly negatively correlated with advice acceptance from an LLM agent <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Colombatto et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond GenAI agents, various studies have examined the relationship between trust and anthropomorphism in other computer-based agents.
The general finding is that as anthropomorphism increases, the trust in the agents increases (Gong, 2008; Nowak, 2004; Waytz et al., 2010; Waytz et al., 2014).
text.formatted: The general finding is that as anthropomorphism increases, the trust in the agents increases <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Gong, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Nowak, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Waytz et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Waytz et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: When participants interacted with a computer agent represented by a static image avatar of varying levels of human-likeness, higher levels of anthropomorphism resulted in the agent being more highly rated for competence and trustworthiness (Gong, 2008).
text.formatted: When participants interacted with a computer agent represented by a static image avatar of varying levels of human-likeness, higher levels of anthropomorphism resulted in the agent being more highly rated for competence and trustworthiness <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Gong, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, when autonomous vehicles in a driving simulation study were given anthropomorphic features (i.e., name, gender, and voice), drivers were more trusting of the vehicle compared with drivers in the non-anthropomorphized condition (Waytz et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Similarly, when autonomous vehicles in a driving simulation study were given anthropomorphic features (i.e., name, gender, and voice), drivers were more trusting of the vehicle compared with drivers in the non-anthropomorphized condition <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Waytz et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Most of these studies conveyed anthropomorphism through static cues: a face or avatar (Gong, 2008; Nowak, 2004), a name, gender, or voice (Cohn et al., 2024; Waytz et al., 2014), or a description (Castelo et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Most of these studies conveyed anthropomorphism through static cues: a face or avatar <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Gong, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Nowak, 2004)</ref>, a name, gender, or voice <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Cohn et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Waytz et al., 2014)</ref>, or a description <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Castelo et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Conversational agents can also convey humanness through their behavior during an interaction, such as informal, responsive language (Araujo, 2018; Go & Sundar, 2019), while expressions of sympathy and empathy can lead people to respond to a chatbot as a social actor (Liu & Sundar, 2018).
text.formatted: Conversational agents can also convey humanness through their behavior during an interaction, such as informal, responsive language <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Araujo, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Go & Sundar, 2019)</ref>, while expressions of sympathy and empathy can lead people to respond to a chatbot as a social actor <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Liu & Sundar, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Although higher levels of anthropomorphism often promote trust, prior research suggests that human-machine trust is shaped by additional cognitive biases.

Phenomena such as automation bias and complacency (Goddard et al., 2012; Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010), algorithm aversion (Dietvorst et al., 2015), and human favoritism (Zhang & Gosline, 2023) highlight that trust in artificial agents depends not only on perceived humanness but also on task context and pre-existing expectations about technology.
text.formatted: Phenomena such as automation bias and complacency <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Goddard et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010)</ref>, algorithm aversion <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Dietvorst et al., 2015)</ref>, and human favoritism <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Zhang & Gosline, 2023)</ref> highlight that trust in artificial agents depends not only on perceived humanness but also on task context and pre-existing expectations about technology.

text.text: Humans demonstrate automation bias when they show an increased willingness to rely on automation without verifying the likely accuracy of its output.

In line with automation bias, De Visser et al. (2016) found that participants initially deferred to a non-anthropomorphized computer agent more readily than to more human-like agents when doing a judgment task.
text.formatted: In line with automation bias, De <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Visser et al. (2016)</ref> found that participants initially deferred to a non-anthropomorphized computer agent more readily than to more human-like agents when doing a judgment task.

text.text: However, trust in the human-like agents was more resilient as the agents' advice became less reliable.
Algorithm aversion shows the opposite pattern: Castelo et al. (2019)found that people trusted algorithms less than humans for tasks that are perceived as subjective, such as writing content.
text.formatted: Algorithm aversion shows the opposite pattern: <ref type="formula">Castelo et al. (2019)</ref>found that people trusted algorithms less than humans for tasks that are perceived as subjective, such as writing content.

text.text: When the algorithms were portrayed as having affective humanlikeness, their perceived usefulness for more subjective tasks increased (Castelo et al., 2019).
text.formatted: When the algorithms were portrayed as having affective humanlikeness, their perceived usefulness for more subjective tasks increased <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Castelo et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: It remains unclear how users may perceive newer systems given the significant development of AI systems in recent years.
Previous research was primarily about purpose-built automation, algorithms, and AI systems.
General-purpose, conversational GenAI agents may invoke different cognitive biases and mechanisms.
For instance, Zhang & Gosline (2023) compared persuasive content generated by human experts, by GenAI, and by the two in collaboration.
text.formatted: For instance, Zhang & Gosline (2023) compared persuasive content generated by human experts, by GenAI, and by the two in collaboration.

text.text: When participants did not know the source, they rated AIgenerated content as higher quality than human-generated content.
When they were told the source, however, content attributed to a human expert was rated more highly than when its source was unknown.
Learning that AI was involved in the writing process did not lower ratings of the content.
These findings suggest that human favoritism, rather than algorithm aversion, may bias judgments of generated content.
Other studies of AI authorship point in different directions.
Readers rated news attributed to a robot reporter as less credible than identical news attributed to a human journalist (Waddell, 2018).
text.formatted: Readers rated news attributed to a robot reporter as less credible than identical news attributed to a human journalist <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Waddell, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Headlines labeled as written by AI were rated as less accurate than the same headlines labeled as written by humans, for both true and false headlines (Longoni et al., 2022; see also Altay & Gilardi, 2024).
text.formatted: Headlines labeled as written by AI were rated as less accurate than the same headlines labeled as written by humans, for both true and false headlines <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Longoni et al., 2022</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Altay & Gilardi, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the machine heuristic proposes that people may assume machine sources are objective and free of bias, which could protect machine-authored content from some of the skepticism directed at human sources (Sundar, 2008).
text.formatted: In contrast, the machine heuristic proposes that people may assume machine sources are objective and free of bias, which could protect machine-authored content from some of the skepticism directed at human sources <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Sundar, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: However, when Waddell (2018) tested this directly, the machine heuristic did not explain how readers judged machine-written news; instead, the lower credibility was partly explained by the machine author seeming less human.
text.formatted: However, when <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Waddell (2018)</ref> tested this directly, the machine heuristic did not explain how readers judged machine-written news; instead, the lower credibility was partly explained by the machine author seeming less human.

text.text: These studies typically measure the credibility of the content alone and rarely ask whether author trust and content trust move together when the presentation of the author changes.

Taken together, these findings highlight a complex relationship between anthropomorphism and trust; while human-like cues can foster trust in automation, biases such as automation bias and human favoritism can complicate the relationship.
Prior work has also largely examined either trust in artificial agents or the credibility of their content, but not how the two respond to the same cues.
The current experiments addressed this by manipulating the anthropomorphic cues of an author and testing directly whether they affect trust in the author and trust in the content to the same degree.
In two experiments, we evaluated how manipulating the anthropomorphic cues of an author affected trust in that author and trust in the content attributed to them.
In all cases, the content was a science communication blog post about a fictional medical breakthrough.
Because the post was the same in every condition, we could test whether author cues affected judgments of the author and the content to the same degree.

Experiment 1 presented one of three authors-a GenAI author with low anthropomorphic cues, a GenAI author with high anthropomorphic cues, or a human expert-using a name, image, and a short description.
Experiment 2 varied whether a GenAI chatbot, presented as the author of the same blog post, exhibited more or fewer anthropomorphic cues during a conversation.
Measuring author and content trust in response to the same manipulations, rather than either one alone, is what allows the two to be compared.
Details of each manipulation are provided within the Methods section of each experiment.
We hypothesized the following: • H1: An increase in anthropomorphic cues would increase the ratings of trustworthiness of the author.
• H2: An increase in anthropomorphic cues would increase the ratings of trustworthiness of the content.

Our findings were consistent with H1 for the comparison between the human and GenAI authors in Experiment 1 and for the behavioral manipulation in Experiment 2, but not for the comparison between the low-and high-anthropomorphic-cue GenAI authors in Experiment 1.
The findings did not support H2.
We did not detect a reliable effect of author presentation on content trust in the primary analyses of either experiment.
In Experiment 1, the effect of author presentation on author trust was reliably larger than its effect on content trust; in Experiment 2, the evidence on this comparison was inconclusive.
Anonymized data, study materials, and analysis scripts for all experiments are available online on the Open Science Framework (OSF) website (https://osf.io/6u74p/).
text.formatted: Anonymized data, study materials, and analysis scripts for all experiments are available online on the Open Science Framework (OSF) website (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/6u74p/">https://osf.io/6u74p/</ref>).

text.text: In Experiment 1, participants read the blog post and a short description of the agent they were told was the author of the post.
They were then asked to report how trustworthy they found the author and the content.
They were also asked to report their perceptions of other characteristics of the author (i.e., anthropomorphism, likeability, and perceived intelligence).
This experiment was approved by a Research Ethics Board of the University of Waterloo (REB #47011) and was not preregistered.
We recruited 315 US-based participants through CloudResearch.
This sample was determined in accordance with a power analysis performed using the pwr package (version 1.3-0; Champely, 2020) in R (version 4.6.1; R Core Team, 2026).
The power analysis indicated that we would need a minimum of 53 participants in each of the three condition levels, for a total of 159, to detect a moderate size effect (Cohen's f = 0.25).
To detect a small effect (Cohen's f = 0.10), we would need to recruit 323 participants per level for a total of 969.

Due to the limited number of existing studies that looked at the effect of anthropomorphic cues in GenAI on epistemic trust, we took a conservative approach and aimed to target the detection of a small to moderate effect while balancing the overall cost of the study.

We aimed to recruit a minimum of 300 participants, 100 in each condition, with the assumption of at most 20% exclusions due to poor data quality and attrition (n = 80, k = 3, Cohen's f = 0.20, α= 0.05, 1 -β≈0.80).
With the final sample, the design had 80% power to detect an omnibus effect of Cohen's f = 0.19 and a pairwise difference of Cohen's d = 0.42 (Cohen's d = 0.49 with Bonferroni correction).
Participants were compensated with US$2.00 for completing this 15-minute online survey.

Participants were from the United States of America, were recruited from the CloudResearch Approved Participants List, and were required to have an approval rating greater than or equal to 95% and to have completed more than 100 HITs.

After data exclusion for quality control (further described in the analysis section), the final sample was 270 participants (ages 21 to 79, Mage = 45.10, SDage = 12.27; 107 females; 268 fluent in English; 256 English as a first language; 232 with at least some post-secondary education).
Conditions did not differ in age, sex, education, or frequency of GenAI use (Kruskal-Wallis tests, all ps > .22; Table 1).
text.formatted: Conditions did not differ in age, sex, education, or frequency of GenAI use (Kruskal-Wallis tests, all ps > .22; Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: They did differ in how often participants consumed media similar to the blog post (p = .025): participants in the low condition were more likely to consume such media at least weekly (54%, compared with 34% and 38% in the high and human conditions respectively).

Participants were presented with a brief description and an accompanying image of an author.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three author description conditions.
Two of the conditions used GenAI agents, and a third provided a human baseline for comparison.

The description and image presented for the author had varying anthropomorphic cues per condition: (1) low anthropomorphic cues: the author, named "Science Communication AI," was described as a GenAI agent in functional, mechanical language and represented by an image of a computer; (2) high anthropomorphic cues: the author, named "Simone the Science Synthesizer," was described as a GenAI agent with human-like attributes (e.g., having emotions) and represented by a human-like cartoon image; and (3) human expert: the author, named "Dr.
Simone Tran," was described as a human science communication expert and represented with a photograph of a person aligned with the description.
We used ChatGPT (GPT-4o) (OpenAI, 2024) to generate the author descriptions for each of the three conditions.
The photographs for the low and human conditions were free-to-use stock images obtained from Pexels (G., 2021; Nikhomkhai, 2016).
text.formatted: The photographs for the low and human conditions were free-to-use stock images obtained from Pexels <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(G., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Nikhomkhai, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The cartoon image used for the high condition was generated by ChatGPT based on the image for the human condition (OpenAI, 2024).
See Figure 1 for the author descriptions and images by condition.
text.formatted: See Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> for the author descriptions and images by condition.

text.text: Because a GenAI author cannot plausibly hold professional credentials, the human condition differed from the GenAI conditions in implied expertise as well as in anthropomorphic cues.

We therefore interpret differences between the human and the two GenAI conditions as differences between kinds of author and treat the comparison between the low and high conditions as the test of anthropomorphic cues within GenAI.
The high and human conditions shared the name Simone and a human-like image, so the difference between them lay mainly in the type of author and the title that signaled expertise.
All participants then read the same fictional science communication blog post, which was presented as written by the author described in their assigned vignette.
The Internet is increasingly a source of scientific information for many.

In the United States, the National Science Board (NSB) reported an increase in Americans saying they use the Internet as their primary source of science and technology news, up from 9% in 2001 to 57% in 2018, with 70% saying they would go online to learn more about a science and technology issue (National Science Board, 2020).

Similarly, Americans view new medical discoveries as the most interesting topic within science and technology news, with 56% of respondents being very interested in them (National Science Board, 2020).
However, determining whether the content on the Internet is reliable and trustworthy is not necessarily straightforward.
Therefore, to support external validity, we chose to use a science communication blog post as the authored content stimulus.

Furthermore, given that Sperber et al. (2010) noted that people are more epistemically vigilant when information is relevant to them, we decided to use a fictional medical breakthrough related to inflammatory diseases which afflict many people worldwide (Slavich, 2015).

(2010)</ref> noted that people are more epistemically vigilant when information is relevant to them, we decided to use a fictional medical breakthrough related to inflammatory diseases which afflict many people worldwide <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Slavich, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: We used ChatGPT (GPT-4o) (OpenAI, 2024) to generate the blog post; all prompts used to generate stimuli are available on OSF.
The post reads as a summary of a placebo-controlled clinical trial conducted by other researchers, and its tone is optimistic.
The full text of the post is available in Figure 2.

text.text: Anthropomorphism was measured using a subset of items from the Godspeed Instrument, which consists of a series of questionnaires developed to measure anthropomorphism, animacy, likeability, perceived intelligence, and perceived safety (Bartneck et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Anthropomorphism was measured using a subset of items from the Godspeed Instrument, which consists of a series of questionnaires developed to measure anthropomorphism, animacy, likeability, perceived intelligence, and perceived safety <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bartneck et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Each trait is measured using a semantic differential scale with relevant anchor descriptives for each item (left descriptive = 0 and right descriptive = 100).
We combined and randomized the items from the anthropomorphism, likeability, and perceived intelligence subsets (e.g., Fake-Natural, Unfriendly-Friendly, Incompetent-Competent).
We removed "Moving rigidly-Moving elegantly" from the anthropomorphism questionnaire because the participants were not interacting with a moving robot.
We used the Muenster Epistemic Trustworthiness Inventory (METI; Hendriks et al., 2015) to assess epistemic trustworthiness of the author of the provided communication content.
text.formatted: We used the Muenster Epistemic Trustworthiness Inventory (METI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Hendriks et al., 2015)</ref> to assess epistemic trustworthiness of the author of the provided communication content.

text.text: The METI was designed to measure epistemic trustworthiness of experts when laypeople are presented with limited information about the expert, such as a short text description (Hendriks et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The METI was designed to measure epistemic trustworthiness of experts when laypeople are presented with limited information about the expert, such as a short text description <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Hendriks et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: It consists of 14 items in three subscales: expertise (6 items), integrity (4 items), and benevolence (4 items).

Each item was measured with a semantic differential scale with a slider anchored between pairs of adjectives (e.g., Honest-Dishonest, Fair-Unfair, Considerate-Inconsiderate; left descriptive = 0 and right descriptive = 100).
Given the similar structure to the Godspeed items, we presented these measures to participants on the same screen, intermixing and randomizing the order of the items.
In addition, we asked participants to rate the credibility of the provided communication content using the message credibility scale developed by Appelman & Sundar (2016).
text.formatted: In addition, we asked participants to rate the credibility of the provided communication content using the message credibility scale developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Appelman & Sundar (2016)</ref>.

text.text: The message credibility scale consists of three items (i.e., accurate, authentic, believable).
Participants were asked to rate how well each of these three adjectives described the content on a 5-point scale.
Three additional adjectives were added to the measure to make it less obvious what we were measuring and to gather perceptions of writing quality (i.e., well-written, boring, engaging).
These additions were used for post hoc analysis and did not contribute to the content trust measurement.
All items were presented on the same page, in a random order, and participants responded on a scale from 1 to 5 with scale labels of "Describes very poorly" to "Describes very well".
As an additional indicator of trust in the content and author, and consistent with our focus on trust judgments in realistic contexts, we included items related to behavioral intentions.

We asked participants to rate a series of statements related to the influence of the content they read (i.e., "If I were to suffer from a relevant medical condition, I am likely to use Velocerin." [the medication announced in the blog post content stimuli]; "I would share the information in the article with a close friend or family member who may benefit from the medication described."
; "I believe the claims made about Velocerin in this article."
; "I do not have confidence in Velocerin based on what I have read."
; "The blog post is not trustworthy enough for me to share on social media, if I were a person who shares links on social media."
; "After reading this blog post I have enough information to make an informed decision about Velocerin."

; "If I were suffering from a relevant medical condition, I would look into Velocerin more after reading this blog post.") and the author (i.e., "I would ask the author of this blog post to summarize scientific content for me in the future."
; "I would read articles by the author of this blog post in the future if they were on a topic that was of interest to me.").
A 7-point Likert scale was used for each scale item, with endpoints labeled "Strongly disagree" and "Strongly agree".
This novel measure was specific to the content of this study and had not previously been validated in the literature.

We refer to the combination of the METI and the novel author items as author trust, but it reflects perceived expertise, integrity, and benevolence of the source and intentions to rely on it, not acceptance of the source's claims.

Likewise, we refer to the combination of the message credibility scale and the novel content items as content trust, but it combines perceived credibility with belief, intended action toward the medication, and judgments of whether the post gave enough information.
For this reason, we also report every main analysis using only the validated scales (METI for author trust and message credibility for content trust).
Internal consistency was high and comparable across the item sets used to assess anthropomorphism, author trust, and content trust (see Table 2).

Participants enrolled in the study on the CloudResearch platform and were redirected to a survey hosted on the Qualtrics platform.
Upon starting the study, participants were presented with an information letter and asked to provide their consent to participate in the study.
To reduce bias during data collection, we used partial disclosure.

We indicated that the study was examining perceptions of communicated information and withheld the intention to investigate the relationship between trust, anthropomorphism, and GenAI until participants completed the study.
Upon consent, participants were randomly assigned to one of three author conditions: low (n = 87), high (n = 92), and human (n = 91).

Participants were first presented with an instruction screen that indicated that they should carefully read the blog post and the author's description on the next screen and that they would later be asked to answer questions about the text.

On the next page, they saw a screen containing an image of the authoring agent, a description of that agent, and the blog post; the author description and image varied according to the assigned author condition, whereas the blog post was the same for all conditions.
Participants were asked to answer basic comprehension check questions about the content.
If they did not answer them correctly, they saw a screen asking them to read the description and the blog post carefully again before proceeding.
They were presented with the same stimuli content screen and comprehension check questions once again.
Following this, they proceeded regardless of the correctness of their responses.

On the next screens, participants were shown the following measures in a randomized order: items from the Godspeed Instrument (14 items; Bartneck et al., 2009) and the METI (14 items; Hendriks et al., 2015), which were intermixed in a randomized order; the message credibility scale (3 items; Appelman & Sundar, 2016) combined with the writing quality items, intermixed in a randomized order; and our novel author and content trust scale developed for this experiment.
text.formatted: On the next screens, participants were shown the following measures in a randomized order: items from the Godspeed Instrument (14 items; <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bartneck et al., 2009)</ref> and the METI (14 items; <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Hendriks et al., 2015)</ref>, which were intermixed in a randomized order; the message credibility scale (3 items; Appelman & Sundar, 2016) combined with the writing quality items, intermixed in a randomized order; and our novel author and content trust scale developed for this experiment.

text.text: These were used to measure perceptions of the author, author trust, and content trust respectively.

Participants were then asked about their familiarity with and use of artificial intelligence technology, how often they consumed media similar to the blog post, and demographic information, including age, sex, gender, language fluency, and educational level.
Participants were asked open-ended questions related to anything they found confusing, the purpose of the study, and whether they experienced technical difficulties.
Finally, participants received a debriefing letter that revealed the full purpose of the study and the condition to which they were assigned and stated that the blog post was fictional.
All data analysis was completed using R (version 4.6.1; R Core Team, 2026).

We used the traditional median imputation technique (Alwateer et al., 2024) to replace missing values for continuous variables with the median value of the corresponding author condition subgroup; the mode was used for any categorical variables.
text.formatted: We used the traditional median imputation technique <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alwateer et al., 2024)</ref> to replace missing values for continuous variables with the median value of the corresponding author condition subgroup; the mode was used for any categorical variables.

text.text: We used the median instead of the mean for continuous variables because the data tended to be skewed and not normally distributed across many of the variables.
Only three item responses were missing, each from a different participant (two in the anthropomorphism and trust measures and one in a writing-quality item).
The items combined into each composite (i.e., Godspeed, METI, Appelman and Sundar, and the novel measure) used different response formats (0-100 sliders, a 5-point scale, and 7-point scales).
As such, we standardized each item as a z-score across all participants in the experiment before averaging items into composite scores.

Because each composite is the mean of z-scored items, its standard deviation is below 1 (author trust SD = 0.84, content trust SD = 0.80), so regression coefficients on the composites are in standardized-item units rather than Cohen's d.

In R, we used the stats package (version 4.6.1; R Core Team, 2026) to conduct all one-way analyses of variance (ANOVAs), Welch's t-tests, and Pearson correlations, and the psych package (version 2.6.5; Revelle, 2026) to calculate Cronbach's α; Cohen's d (with the pooled standard deviation) and ω 2 were calculated with functions written for this study.
For all pairwise and post-hoc t-tests, p values were adjusted using Bonferroni correction.

Throughout the paper, condition comparisons are computed as high minus low, human minus low, and human minus high, so positive values of t, d, and B indicate higher scores in the high or human condition.
We fit linear mixed-effects models with the lme4 (version 2.0-1; Bates et al., 2015) and lmerTest (version 3.2-1; Kuznetsova et al., 2017) packages.
Confidence intervals for Cohen's d were computed with the large-sample normal approximation.
Figures were made with the ggplot2 (version 4.0.3; Wickham, 2016) and ggpubr (version 0.6.3; Kassambara, 2026) packages.

We checked the main results in five ways: using only the validated scales, standardizing each composite before comparing author and content trust, adjusting for pre-existing participant characteristics, analyzing complete cases only, and excluding participants who needed to reread the stimuli.

The adjusted models controlled for age, sex (female vs. all other responses), post-secondary education, frequency of GenAI use, and frequency of consuming media similar to the blog post (the latter two as three-level factors: at least weekly, occasionally, or rarely or never), with HC3 robust standard errors (sandwich, version 3.1-1, Zeileis et al., 2020; lmtest, version 0.9-40, Zeileis & Hothorn, 2002; and car, version 3.1-5, Fox & Weisberg, 2019).

From the initial 315 participants, those who did not progress through the complete survey were excluded from the analysis (n = 22).
If a participant skipped individual questions or scale items, their responses were included in the analysis with the missing values imputed as described in the analysis section.

To gauge whether the participant read and understood the stimuli content, the study included three comprehension check questions based on the blog post and author descriptions of the stimuli (e.g., "What was the author?"
with response options "a generative AI agent" or "a human expert").
Twenty-one participants incorrectly answered these questions and were asked to reread the stimuli before answering the questions a second time.
We excluded data from participants who incorrectly answered any of these questions after the second attempt (n = 5).
Participants who correctly answered the questions after the second attempt were included in the final analysis.
An exploratory analysis that excluded these participants confirmed that their inclusion did not alter the pattern of findings reported below (see Table 3).

text.text: To ensure that participants read the questions and prompts attentively throughout the study, we included attention check items within the scales.
These questions consisted of a prompt to select a particular answer (e.g., set the slider to the far right).
Data from participants with incorrect values for any of these questions were excluded from the analysis (n = 16).
We used the Bot Detection feature provided within the Qualtrics platform to screen for potential bot activity (Qualtrics, 2025); no participants were excluded.foot_0

text.text: We fit a linear mixed-effects model predicting trust ratings from author condition, trust type (author or content), and their interaction with random intercepts for participants.
This analysis revealed a significant interaction between condition and trust type, indicating the difference between author trust and content trust varied between author conditions.

text.text: Taken together, these results show that replacing the GenAI author with a human expert influenced trust judgments about the author more than trust judgments about the content itself.

The absence of a significant content trust effect does not mean that the effect was zero.

The high and low conditions produced statistically equivalent content trust at a bound of ±0.30 SD (d = 0.01, 90% CI [-0.24, 0.26], TOST p = .027), but not at ±0.20 (Appendix B); because these two conditions also did not differ in anthropomorphism ratings, this does not show that a successful anthropomorphism manipulation would leave content trust unchanged.
For the human condition, the 90% CI for the content trust difference ([0.00, 0.50]) included effects larger than ±0.30, so a small positive effect cannot be ruled out.
