text.text: The author trust effect and the difference between the author and content trust effects were significant in every specification.
The content trust effect was not significant in four of the five specifications but was significant after covariate adjustment (B = 0.30, p = .008).

Most of this change came from adjusting for how often participants consumed media similar to the blog post, which was imbalanced across conditions (Section 4.1.1); adjusting for that variable alone gave B = 0.29, p = .012, whereas adjusting for all other covariates without it gave B = 0.21, p = .064.

The human author may therefore have had a small positive effect on content trust as well, but the effect on author trust was more than twice as large, and the difference between the two remained significant (B = 0.36, p < .001).
text.formatted: The human author may therefore have had a small positive effect on content trust as well, but the effect on author trust was more than twice as large, and the difference between the two remained significant (B = 0.36, p < .001).

text.text: Across all specifications, the low and high conditions never differed on author trust, content trust, or their difference (all ps > .27).
text.formatted: Across all specifications, the low and high conditions never differed on author trust, content trust, or their difference (all ps > .27).

text.text: Because the manipulation of anthropomorphic cues did not effectively dissociate the low from high conditions (see Section 4.2.2), we followed up our main analysis with a correlational examination of the relationships among anthropomorphism, author trust, and content trust.
All correlations are Pearson's r.
Anthropomorphism was positively correlated with both content trust (r(268) = .49, p < .001, 95% CI [.39, .57]) and author trust (r(268) = .70, p < .001, 95% CI [.64, .76]).
text.formatted: Anthropomorphism was positively correlated with both content trust (r(268) = .49, p < .001, 95% CI [.39, .57]) and author trust (r(268) = .70, p < .001, 95% CI [.64, .76]).

text.text: Author trust and content trust were also strongly, positively correlated (r(268) = .78, p < .001, 95% CI [.73, .83]).
text.formatted: Author trust and content trust were also strongly, positively correlated (r(268) = .78, p < .001, 95% CI [.73, .83]).

text.text: Because these pooled correlations include the differences between conditions produced by the manipulation, we also computed them within conditions (centering each variable on its condition mean, with degrees of freedom adjusted for the condition means removed).

The pattern was similar: anthropomorphism was positively correlated with author trust (r(266) = .66, p < .001, 95% CI [.59, .72]) and with content trust (r(266) = .54, p < .001, 95% CI [.45, .62]), and author trust and content trust were strongly, positively correlated (r(266) = .80, p < .001, 95% CI [.75, .84]).
text.formatted: The pattern was similar: anthropomorphism was positively correlated with author trust (r(266) = .66, p < .001, 95% CI [.59, .72]) and with content trust (r(266) = .54, p < .001, 95% CI [.45, .62]), and author trust and content trust were strongly, positively correlated (r(266) = .80, p < .001, 95% CI [.75, .84]).

text.text: Anthropomorphism was more strongly correlated with author trust than with content trust (Williams's t(265) = 4.29, p < .001).
text.formatted: Anthropomorphism was more strongly correlated with author trust than with content trust (Williams's t(265) = 4.29, p < .001).

text.text: These correlations show that people who saw the author as more human-like also tended to trust both the author and the content more.
They do not show which judgment influenced which (see Section 6.1.1).
To extend the findings of Experiment 1, we ran a follow-up experiment with modifications to the procedure to improve the efficacy of the anthropomorphic cue manipulation.
Our manipulation of anthropomorphic cues in Experiment 1 did not have the intended effect on the perception of anthropomorphism.

We intended that through the manipulation of the descriptions and images of the GenAI agents, participants would have perceptions of anthropomorphism that aligned with their assigned condition (i.e., the mean anthropomorphism score would be lower for the low condition than the high condition).
While there was a significant effect of the anthropomorphic cue manipulation on anthropomorphism, it was only evident between the human condition and each of the GenAI agent conditions.
We did not find a significant difference in the ratings between the two GenAI agent conditions (see Section 4.2.2).
We suspected that reading a description of an agent was not enough to override past experience with similar agents or deep-seated beliefs about non-human agent capabilities.

Changing impressions, especially implicit impressions, can be challenging and require significant and believable counter-evidence for individuals to update their existing impressions of an agent (Ferguson et al., 2019; Mann & Ferguson, 2015).
text.formatted: Changing impressions, especially implicit impressions, can be challenging and require significant and believable counter-evidence for individuals to update their existing impressions of an agent <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Ferguson et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Mann & Ferguson, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: As such, we refined the design in Experiment 2 to see whether a more interactive experience with the author would yield the intended anthropomorphic effects.
The manipulation was more effective with this paradigm as shown in Section 5.2.2.
This experiment used an interactive GenAI chatbot to represent the author agent to provide participants with a more externally valid experience.

The chatbot was instructed to respond with varying levels of anthropomorphic cues during conversation to manipulate the author condition, rather than having participants read descriptive vignettes with avatars.
Additionally, we simplified the anthropomorphic cue manipulation to include only two levels, eliminating the human condition, so that the author was always a GenAI agent.
This experiment was approved by a Research Ethics Board of the University of Waterloo (REB #47304) and was preregistered at https://aspredicted.org/n9sg-nwjx.pdf (AsPredicted #215144).
text.formatted: This experiment was approved by a Research Ethics Board of the University of Waterloo (REB #47304) and was preregistered at <ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/n9sg-nwjx.pdf">https://aspredicted.org/n9sg-nwjx.pdf</ref> (AsPredicted #215144).

text.text: The preregistration specified the hypothesis that increasing anthropomorphism would increase trust in the GenAI author and in its content, the composite measures of author and content trust, the two conditions, a test of the main effect of condition on each trust measure, the exclusion rules, and the sample size.
Section 5.2.1 describes where our analyses departed from it.

A sample of 202 participants was recruited through SONA at the University of Waterloo in accordance with a power analysis carried out using the pwr package (version 1.3-0; Champely, 2020) in R (version 4.6.1; R Core Team, 2026).
Similar to Experiment 1, we targeted a sample large enough to detect a small to moderate effect.
The power analysis indicated we would need between n = 64 (Cohen's f = 0.25) and n = 394 (Cohen's f = 0.10) participants in each of the two condition levels.

The final recruitment sample size was chosen to balance our desired detection ability and the availability of participants within the sample pool; as preregistered, we planned to recruit 200 participants or to stop on March 21, 2025, whichever came first.
Remuneration was 0.5 credits for completing the 30-minute online survey.
After data exclusion for quality control, the final sample was 148 participants (ages 18 to 59, Mage = 20.39, SDage = 4.40; 115 females).
With 75 and 73 participants in the low and high conditions, the design had 80% power to detect a difference of d = 0.47 between conditions.
Most participants used GenAI chatbots at least weekly (74%), and conditions did not differ on any measured characteristic (all ps > .09; Table 1).
text.formatted: Most participants used GenAI chatbots at least weekly (74%), and conditions did not differ on any measured characteristic (all ps > .09; Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Because nearly all participants were undergraduate students in a narrow age range, this sample differs from the Experiment 1 sample in age, education, and GenAI experience.
An interactive chatbot was included instead of the descriptive author vignette and image.
Participants saw a text box where they could enter their message and a larger box where the conversation history was displayed, including the chatbot's responses to their messages (see Figure 5).
text.formatted: Participants saw a text box where they could enter their message and a larger box where the conversation history was displayed, including the chatbot's responses to their messages (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">5</ref>).

text.text: All participants saw the same interface and were required to complete three conversation turns before proceeding.
The chatbot's GenAI functionality was created using Claude Haiku 3.5 model (Anthropic, 2024).
text.formatted: The chatbot's GenAI functionality was created using Claude Haiku 3.5 model <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anthropic, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Differences in the low and high author conditions were controlled through system messages to the API.
To generate responses, the chatbot used the Anthropic API to access the Claude Haiku 3.5 model (claude-3-5-haiku-20241022, temperature 0.5; Anthropic, 2024).
There were two versions of the chatbot, one for each of the two anthropomorphic cue manipulation levels.

Both versions received the same core system prompt, which described the chatbot as an AI science communicator, included the full text of the blog post, stated that the chatbot had written it, and instructed it to claim authorship if asked.
Both versions were limited to responses of two sentences.
Anthropomorphic cue level was manipulated by changing the system prompt to instruct the chatbot to respond in either a more human-like or a more machine-like manner.
Drawing on findings from prior work (Sections 2.3 and 2.4), we instructed the chatbot to express different levels of empathy and emotional understanding.
These expressions were intended to elicit the perception that the chatbot has a mind, making it seem more human-like.

The low author condition chatbot was named "AI science communication"foot_1 and was instructed to respond in a more machine-like manner: to use non-anthropomorphic language, to avoid filler language, and not to express empathy.
text.formatted: The low author condition chatbot was named "AI science communication"<ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">foot_1</ref> and was instructed to respond in a more machine-like manner: to use non-anthropomorphic language, to avoid filler language, and not to express empathy.

text.text: The high author condition chatbot was named "Simone the Science Synthesizer" and was instructed to respond in a more human-like manner, i.e., to pretend it had emotions and understood the emotions of others, to respond empathetically, and such.
See Appendix A for the system prompts used to define the chatbots.
We describe what the conversations contained in Section 5.2.5.
The dependent measures were identical to Experiment 1, except one duplicated scale item from the combination of the Godspeed and METI scales was removed in Experiment 2.

Two additional author trust items were added to the novel trust measure: "I would pay for content written by this author if the topic was of interest to me." and "I trust the author to provide quality information."
The language demographics question was removed because it was of limited use in Experiment 1.
Internal consistency was acceptable to high across the item sets used to assess anthropomorphism, author trust, and content trust (see Table 4).
text.formatted: Internal consistency was acceptable to high across the item sets used to assess anthropomorphism, author trust, and content trust (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">4</ref>).

text.text: Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: low (n = 75) or high (n = 73) anthropomorphic cues.

After participants read the blog post, they were given the opportunity to chat with the GenAI bot, which was programmed to respond according to the participant's assigned condition; they were told they were going to chat with the GenAI author of the blog post and were instructed to have a conversation on the topic of their choice with the bot.
They were required to complete a minimum of three conversational turns before proceeding with the remainder of the experiment.
The participants then completed the same questionnaires as in Experiment 1, with the modifications noted in the Materials section.

All score calculation and analysis followed the same procedures as Experiment 1, except that the main analysis was performed with Welch's t-tests instead of ANOVA since there were only two levels of the anthropomorphic cue manipulation.
Because each outcome involved a single comparison, no within-outcome correction was applied.
The composite standard deviations were 0.58 for author trust and 0.63 for content trust.
To describe the conversations, we used automated keyword counts.

For each chatbot response, we counted words, exclamation marks, emotion words (e.g., excited, glad, sorry, feel, wonderful), and first-and second-person pronouns, and compared conditions with response-level regressions using standard errors clustered by participant.

For each conversation, we flagged whether the participant or the chatbot referred to the blog post, Velocerin, or the underlying study; whether the participant asked about the chatbot's identity or authorship; and whether the chatbot used its fallback reply for missing information, comparing conditions with Fisher's exact tests.
These keyword rules were not validated against human coding.

We followed the same exclusion methods as defined in Experiment 1: failure to complete the survey (n = 12), survey duration less than one-third of the median time to complete (n = 1), failure to pass a content comprehension check (n = 11), and survey attention checks (n = 29).
No participants were excluded as a result of the bot detection check.
An additional participant was removed because they indicated they had not read the blog post before proceeding (n = 1).
This exclusion was decided after reviewing the open-ended responses; retaining this participant did not change the results (Table 5).
text.formatted: This exclusion was decided after reviewing the open-ended responses; retaining this participant did not change the results (Table <ref type="table">5</ref>).

text.text: Before these exclusions, we removed two people who did not consent.
In addition, five participants took the survey more than once (six additional records).
For each, we kept their first complete attempt, or their first attempt if none was complete; four of them had abandoned an earlier attempt before answering any study questions.
Exclusions were balanced across conditions (27 per condition; Appendix B).
Eighty-three item responses were missing across 15 participants and were imputed as in Experiment 1; analyses of the 133 participants with complete data gave the same pattern (Table 5).
text.formatted: Eighty-three item responses were missing across 15 participants and were imputed as in Experiment 1; analyses of the 133 participants with complete data gave the same pattern (Table <ref type="table">5</ref>).

text.text: These exclusions departed from the preregistration, which specified incomplete surveys, failed attention checks, reCAPTCHA scores below 0, and random characters in openended responses.

We also applied the completion time and comprehension check exclusions from Experiment 1, used the reCAPTCHA threshold of 0.5 recommended by Qualtrics (which excluded no one), and excluded the participant described above.
The preregistration did not address repeat participation, which we handled as described above.

Applying only the preregistered rules, with the same handling of repeat participation, leaves 154 participants (78 low, 76 high) and gives the same pattern: author trust d = 0.38, 95% CI [0.06, 0.70], p = .019; content trust d = 0.14, 95% CI [-0.18, 0.45], p = .40 (Appendix B).
We analyzed the main effects with Welch's t-tests rather than the preregistered ANOVA.

With two groups, the ANOVA is equivalent to Student's t-test, and because the groups were nearly equal in size, Student's and Welch's tests gave practically identical results (largest difference in p: < .001).
text.formatted: With two groups, the ANOVA is equivalent to Student's t-test, and because the groups were nearly equal in size, Student's and Welch's tests gave practically identical results (largest difference in p: < .001).

text.text: The test of whether condition affected author trust more than content trust, the robustness models, the equivalence tests, the within-condition correlations and comparison of dependent correlations, and the conversation analyses were not preregistered and should be considered exploratory.
The preregistered correlations between the main measures and sample characteristics are reported in Appendix B.

A t-test comparing the anthropomorphism score means across the high (n = 73, M = 0.26, SD = 0.72) and low (n = 75, M = -0.25, SD = 0.92) conditions showed a moderately sized significant effect of the manipulation on anthropomorphism (t(139.72) = 3.73, p < .001, d = 0.61, 95% CI [0.28, 0.94]).

text.text: In contrast, there was a significant effect of the anthropomorphic cue manipulation, with higher trust for the agent programmed to show high (n = 73, M = 0.12, SD = 0.53) vs. low (n = 75, M = -0.12, SD = 0.60) anthropomorphic cues (t(144.90) = 2.61, p = .010, d = 0.43, 95% CI [0.10, 0.75]) as shown in Figure 7.

text.text: Similar to Experiment 1, we fit a linear mixed-effects model to test for differing effects of the anthropomorphic cue manipulation on author and content trust.
This analysis did not reveal a significant interaction between condition and trust type.
Specifically, the difference between author and content trust in the high author condition did not differ significantly from that observed in the low author condition (t(146) = 1.30, p = .196).

This difference corresponds to about 0.2 standard deviations of the author-minus-content difference, and the design had only about 25% power to detect a difference of that size; the nonsignificant interaction therefore does not show that the manipulation affected author and content trust to a similar extent.

With the validated scales alone, the high condition chatbot again received higher METI scores, d = 0.45, 95% CI [0.12, 0.77], p = .007, with no reliable difference in message credibility, d = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.26, 0.38], p = .72; the difference between these effects was not significant, t(146) = 1.76, p = .080.

In exploratory analyses of the METI subscales, the author trust effects were d = 0.40, 95% CI [0.07, 0.72], for expertise, d = 0.44 [0.11, 0.76] for integrity, and d = 0.30 [-0.02, 0.63] for benevolence (Appendix B); we did not test whether the subscale effects differ.
Perceived writing quality did not differ, d = 0.25, p = .13.
The absence of a significant content trust effect again does not mean the effect was zero.

Its 95% confidence interval extended to about d = 0.5, and equivalence tests established that the content trust effect was negligible only at the widest bound we examined (±0.50; message credibility at ±0.40 or wider; Appendix B).
The author trust effect was significant in all five specifications, with similar estimates across them (B from 0.23 to 0.28; Table 5).
text.formatted: The author trust effect was significant in all five specifications, with similar estimates across them (B from 0.23 to 0.28; Table <ref type="table">5</ref>).

text.text: The content trust effect was small and not significant in every specification, and the difference between the two effects was not significant in any of the specifications in Table 5.
text.formatted: The content trust effect was small and not significant in every specification, and the difference between the two effects was not significant in any of the specifications in Table <ref type="table">5</ref>.

text.text: When each composite was standardized before comparison, the difference remained nonsignificant for the combined composites (B = 0.22, p = .14) but was significant for the validated scales (B = 0.38, 95% CI [0.02, 0.73], p = .036; Appendix B).
This is exploratory evidence in the expected direction, but it appeared in one of several specifications and not in the others.

Similar to Experiment 1, we followed up our main analysis by looking at the correlation between anthropomorphism and our other variables of interest.
We calculated Pearson correlation coefficients for all correlational analyses.
Anthropomorphism was positively correlated with both content trust (r(146) = .42, p < .001, 95% CI [.28, .55]) and author trust (r(146) = .44, p < .001, 95% CI [.30, .56]).

text.text: Within conditions (centering each variable on its condition mean, as in Experiment 1), the correlations were nearly identical: anthropomorphism was positively correlated with content trust (r(145) = .41, p < .001, 95% CI [.27, .54]) and with author trust (r(145) = .41, p < .001, 95% CI [.26, .53]), and author trust was positively correlated with content trust (r(145) = .57, p < .001, 95% CI [.45, .67]).

text.text: Unlike in Experiment 1, anthropomorphism was no more strongly correlated with author trust than with content trust (Williams's t(144) = -0.08, p = .94).
Overall, these results were consistent in direction with Experiment 1: the more human-like chatbot received higher author trust, and no reliable content trust effect was detected.

However, the difference between the two effects was not significant, so Experiment 2 is inconclusive on its own about whether anthropomorphic cues within GenAI affect author and content trust differently.
General Discussion, Limitations, and Future Directions
In general, and aligning with past research, we found a positive correlational relationship between anthropomorphism and trust for the author and the content it produces.

In Experiment 1, replacing a GenAI author with a human expert, a comparison between kinds of author rather than of anthropomorphism alone, shifted evaluations of the author more than evaluations of the post attributed to it.
Experiment 2 was consistent in direction but inconclusive about whether behavioral cues affected the two forms of trust differently.
Contrary to H2, then, we found no reliable evidence that anthropomorphic cues increase content trust.
Past research has highlighted that confidence in information partially depends on judgments of source trustworthiness (e.g., Li et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Past research has highlighted that confidence in information partially depends on judgments of source trustworthiness (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Li et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Our data are consistent with this in one sense: author and content trust were strongly correlated in both experiments.
Because the two were measured at the same time, these correlations cannot show that author trust transmits the effect of author cues to content trust.
Moreover, in Experiment 1, author type (GenAI vs. human) affected author trust much more than content trust.
Several accounts could explain this divergence.
Our design cannot distinguish them, but each makes a prediction that future studies could test.
First, the message carried its own epistemic cues.

Theories of epistemic vigilance hold that people weigh what is said as well as who says it, and that social cues about the source matter most when epistemic cues are scarce (Li et al., 2023; Sperber et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Theories of epistemic vigilance hold that people weigh what is said as well as who says it, and that social cues about the source matter most when epistemic cues are scarce <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Li et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Sperber et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Our post named a mechanism, a trial size, a placebo comparison, and specific outcomes, and every participant read the same content, so the cues that varied by condition were mostly informative about the author rather than about the claims.
This account predicts larger transfer from author to content when messages are short, vague, or hard to evaluate, unlike the detailed post used here.
Second, the author relayed rather than produced the evidence.
The post presented itself as a summary of a trial conducted by other researchers, so the credibility of its claims could rest on that trial rather than on whoever summarized it.
People may be comfortable with AI summarizing information they would not trust AI to produce.
This account predicts that author cues would matter more for content trust if the GenAI were presented as the source of the evidence rather than as a summarizer of it.

Third, the largest effect in our data, the difference in author trust between the human expert and the GenAI authors, may reflect credit for the human author, a penalty for the GenAI authors, or both; without a condition with no attributed author, we cannot tell which.

The corresponding content trust effect (d = 0.25) is in the same direction as the content penalties reported for AI-labeled news and headlines and is similarly modest (Longoni et al., 2022; Waddell, 2018).
text.formatted: The corresponding content trust effect (d = 0.25) is in the same direction as the content penalties reported for AI-labeled news and headlines and is similarly modest <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Longoni et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Waddell, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Human favoritism (Zhang & Gosline, 2023) and a machine heuristic that treats machine sources as objective (Sundar, 2008) are both compatible with this pattern.
text.formatted: Human favoritism <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Zhang & Gosline, 2023)</ref> and a machine heuristic that treats machine sources as objective <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Sundar, 2008)</ref> are both compatible with this pattern.

text.text: Finally, some of the divergence may reflect measurement.
Anthropomorphism and author trust were rated on the same page in the same slider format, whereas content trust was rated on separate pages with different response formats.
This would inflate correlations among the author measures, although it less clearly explains the condition effects, because the dissociation held with the validated scales alone.

The pattern of correlations also differed between experiments: in Experiment 1, anthropomorphism was more strongly related to author trust than to content trust, whereas in Experiment 2 it was related to both to a similar degree, although the experiments also differed in population and cues.

One possibility is that the differences in experimental methods, passively reading a description of the author (Experiment 1) versus interacting with a chatbot (Experiment 2), engaged differing cognitive mechanisms underlying trustworthiness judgments for agents we directly interact with (vs. simply learn about).
In Experiment 2, participants interacted directly with a GenAI agent they were told was the author, likely increasing the salience of the authoring agent.
Social presence theory proposes that interpersonal cues play a stronger role in judgments when a source feels more present (Cui et al., 2013; Short, 1976).
text.formatted: Social presence theory proposes that interpersonal cues play a stronger role in judgments when a source feels more present <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Cui et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Short, 1976)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with social presence theory (Short, 1976) and attribution theory, the increased salience of author characteristics could have led participants to rely more directly on interpersonal trust cues when judging the content (Fiske et al., 1982; Nass & Moon, 2000).
text.formatted: Consistent with social presence theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Short, 1976)</ref> and attribution theory, the increased salience of author characteristics could have led participants to rely more directly on interpersonal trust cues when judging the content <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Fiske et al., 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Nass & Moon, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, in Experiment 1, where the author was less salient, attribution may have relied more on heuristic-based trust judgments, such as algorithm aversion or human favoritism, which are known to shape trust and credibility judgments (Dietvorst et al., 2015; Morewedge, 2022).
text.formatted: In contrast, in Experiment 1, where the author was less salient, attribution may have relied more on heuristic-based trust judgments, such as algorithm aversion or human favoritism, which are known to shape trust and credibility judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Dietvorst et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Morewedge, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the salience of the author could account for the different relationship between content trust and anthropomorphism between experiments.
Beyond social presence, differences in cognitive engagement may also have contributed to these divergent effects in the correlational relationships across experiments.
Experiment 1 involved passive reading, potentially leading to shallow processing of the content, while the interaction with the chatbot in Experiment 2 may have prompted deeper engagement.

In the Elaboration Likelihood Model, Petty & Cacioppo (1986) postulate that when one is more motivated and able to consider communications deeply, they are likely to consider the content of the message rather than relying on peripheral cues, and conversely that shallow processing results in dependency on these external cues.
text.formatted: In the Elaboration Likelihood Model, <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Petty & Cacioppo (1986)</ref> postulate that when one is more motivated and able to consider communications deeply, they are likely to consider the content of the message rather than relying on peripheral cues, and conversely that shallow processing results in dependency on these external cues.

text.text: Thus, the deeper processing may have triggered different cognitive mechanisms to be used in the trust judgments.
Another possible explanation lies not in the manipulation itself but in participants' beliefs about the plausibility of the GenAI author.
Some participants noted that they did not believe that the GenAI agent could have authored the blog post.
Other participants may have held similar beliefs without sharing this information with us.
This is especially probable in Experiment 1, where participants read a description of an agent that may not have matched with their prior experience or beliefs.
The potential expectancy violation and disbelief that participants may have experienced could also have suppressed potential effects of anthropomorphism on content trust.

And when participants had the chance to interact with the GenAI chatbot, particularly the one in the high condition, they could see evidence that the writing ability was aligned to that necessary to write the blog post.
In Experiment 2, only one participant spontaneously reported doubting that the AI had written the post, although we did not ask about this directly.
This difference in believability could explain the difference in correlations between anthropomorphism and content trust across experiments.
A strength of this research is that it tested the same question with two designs: a written description of the author (Experiment 1) and a live conversation with it (Experiment 2).

In both, the author's presentation affected author trust more than content trust, reliably so only in Experiment 1, and the two forms of trust were strongly correlated, so these patterns do not depend on a single paradigm.
The two operationalizations produced different results.

A human-like description of a GenAI author produced no detectable difference in perceived humanness, likeability, or trust, whereas human-like behavior during a conversation made the chatbot seem more human and likeable.
Because the experiments also differed in population and cues, this contrast does not show that behavioral cues are more effective than descriptive ones.
The behavioral manipulation also changed some perceptions more clearly than others.

The empathetic chatbot was rated as clearly more likeable, whereas the difference in Godspeed perceived intelligence was smaller and not significant; yet the METI expertise subscale, which asks about the author's competence as a source of information, showed a modest effect, as did integrity (Section 5.2.3).
These results therefore do not show that the manipulation affected warmth rather than competence.

Because attributions of intelligence, rather than of emotion or experience, predict advice taking from large language models (Colombatto et al., 2025), manipulations that vary warmth and perceived competence separately would help clarify which, if either, carries over to message credibility.
text.formatted: Because attributions of intelligence, rather than of emotion or experience, predict advice taking from large language models <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Colombatto et al., 2025)</ref>, manipulations that vary warmth and perceived competence separately would help clarify which, if either, carries over to message credibility.

text.text: We also saw little sign of algorithm aversion toward the GenAI authors' content: ratings of the post differed only modestly between human and GenAI authors.
Algorithm aversion is strongest for tasks people see as subjective (Castelo et al., 2019) and after an algorithm makes a visible error (Dietvorst et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Algorithm aversion is strongest for tasks people see as subjective <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Castelo et al., 2019)</ref> and after an algorithm makes a visible error <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Dietvorst et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Summarizing a research study may be seen as an objective task, and in Experiment 1 participants had no opportunity to observe an error.

Similar credibility ratings for human and GenAI authors also do not by themselves indicate automation bias or inappropriate reliance (Goddard et al., 2012; Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010); that question requires measures of reliance on information whose accuracy is known.
text.formatted: Similar credibility ratings for human and GenAI authors also do not by themselves indicate automation bias or inappropriate reliance <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Goddard et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010)</ref>; that question requires measures of reliance on information whose accuracy is known.

text.text: The clearest result for designers is that replacing a GenAI author with a human expert shifted evaluations of the source more than evaluations of the message it delivered.
Whether the same holds for changes in how a GenAI system itself is presented needs confirmation, because our evidence within GenAI was weak.

If it does, favorable impressions of a system may still shape whether people keep using it or rely on it across many interactions, so human-like style should not be treated as a proxy for reliability.
Interfaces that support calibrated trust, such as provenance information, citations, and expressions of uncertainty, address message credibility more directly than social cues do.

For researchers, the results argue for measuring trust in a system and trust in its content separately: a study that measured only one of them would reach a different conclusion about the effect of author presentation than a study that measured only the other.
While these findings help clarify the role of anthropomorphism in shaping epistemic trust, some methodological and contextual limitations warrant consideration.
First, Experiment 1 did not isolate anthropomorphism.

The human condition differed from the GenAI conditions in the type of author and in implied expertise as well as in anthropomorphic cues, and the two GenAI conditions did not differ in anthropomorphism ratings.

Because a GenAI author cannot plausibly hold professional credentials, separating humanness from expertise would require holding expertise constant in another way, for example by describing every author with the same role and experience and no title, and including a condition with no attributed author.
Although the interactive chatbot was a more externally valid method of interacting with GenAI in general, it was less realistic for general consumption of science content from the Internet.
We think this was an appropriate trade-off to make in order to test the hypothesis that the direct interaction with the agent would more effectively trigger anthropomorphism.

The manipulation, however, changed more than humanness: the high condition chatbot was more likeable, gave longer responses, and had a different name, and participants received different additional information during their conversations.
We did not assess whether the chatbots added unsupported details or made factual errors.
Future studies may want to delve into exploring the emergence of anthropomorphism and the mechanisms of mind perception in non-embodied agents.

As demonstrated by the different results of Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 in relation to the anthropomorphic cue manipulation achieving the expected change in anthropomorphism ratings, not every anthropomorphic cue manipulation will be effective for GenAI agents.
Further exploration of what cues people are susceptible to when forming anthropomorphic impressions of agents is critical to inform our understanding of potential risks of GenAI agent design.

The two experiments also differed in population (online adults versus undergraduate students), and Experiment 2 was underpowered for the comparison between author and content trust; roughly 300 participants per condition would be needed to detect a difference of the size we observed with 80% power.
Experiment 1 was not preregistered, several analyses in both experiments were exploratory, and the equivalence bounds were chosen after data collection.
Additionally, there are individual differences in the tendency to anthropomorphize agents (Waytz et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Additionally, there are individual differences in the tendency to anthropomorphize agents <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Waytz et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: We used a between-subjects design to avoid potential carryover effects between conditions, but in doing so also introduced variability due to individual differences between participants.

Ideally, we would have collected data from participants to be able to test the impact of these individual differences but, balancing the risk of survey fatigue, chose not to include an additional survey such as the Individual Differences in Anthropomorphism Questionnaire (IDAQ; Waytz et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Ideally, we would have collected data from participants to be able to test the impact of these individual differences but, balancing the risk of survey fatigue, chose not to include an additional survey such as the Individual Differences in Anthropomorphism Questionnaire (IDAQ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Waytz et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: We also measured prior GenAI use but not AI literacy or technical self-efficacy, which may moderate how people respond to human-like AI.
Future research should explore using measures such as the IDAQ or a within-subjects design with suitable precautions taken to prevent carryover effects between conditions.
All outcomes were self-reported ratings collected in a single session.

The author trust composite combines perceived expertise, integrity, and benevolence with intentions to rely on the author, and the content trust composite combines perceived credibility with belief and intended action; neither is a direct measure of accepting communicated knowledge.
The novel items have not been independently validated, although our conclusions held with the validated scales alone.
Additionally, we chose one particular type of content (i.e., science content about medical research aimed at lay people) to focus our research on for simplicity and consistency.
Holding the message constant across conditions is what allowed us to compare author and content trust, but using a single, optimistic message limits generalization.

It is entirely plausible that the relationship between anthropomorphism and content trust may vary across contexts; in particular, the results may not generalize to subjective content, such as creative writing or opinion, for which people are more averse to algorithmic sources (Castelo et al., 2019).
text.formatted: It is entirely plausible that the relationship between anthropomorphism and content trust may vary across contexts; in particular, the results may not generalize to subjective content, such as creative writing or opinion, for which people are more averse to algorithmic sources <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Castelo et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: And as highlighted by Sperber et al. (2010), subject matter that is less relevant to a participant reduces the need for epistemic trust.
text.formatted: And as highlighted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Sperber et al. (2010)</ref>, subject matter that is less relevant to a participant reduces the need for epistemic trust.

text.text: Exploration of different types of content, which may have different relevance to participants, is necessary before general conclusions can be drawn about the relationship between anthropomorphism and content trust.
Furthermore, these studies included only a plausibly credible, fictional blog post as the content stimuli.

Future studies may consider using an article that provides misinformation, disinformation, or a conspiracy theory to see whether the epistemic trustworthiness of such content is affected similarly based on anthropomorphism of the authoring agent.
While these experiments focused on anthropomorphism, future studies could explore other factors that may influence epistemic trust in GenAI content.

Some potential factors that could be interesting to explore are interactivity, organizational credibility, transparency and explainability of content, content domain, social cues from peers or experts (e.g., reviews, endorsements), and communication style (e.g., tone, style, empathy).
As GenAI becomes increasingly embedded in the information ecosystem, understanding how to foster appropriate levels of epistemic trust is essential.
Across two experiments, how human-like an author appeared to be affected how much people trusted the author more than how much they trusted what it wrote.
This was clearest when the author was a human expert rather than a GenAI agent.
Participants trusted the human author more, while there was not a significant difference in how much they trusted the same blog post.
Among GenAI authors, describing the AI as more human-like had no detectable effect.
However, a chatbot that behaved in an empathetic, emotionally expressive way was seen as more human-like and was trusted modestly more as an author.
Experiment 2 was underpowered to test whether this behavior affected trust in the author and trust in the content differently.
This work underscores the need to distinguish between trust in agents and trust in information, especially as GenAI becomes more integrated into communication and education settings.
Understanding how people come to trust-not only GenAI agents, but also the content they produce-is critical for combating misplaced trust in potentially unreliable content and over-reliance on GenAI.

text.text: Both chatbots received the same core prompt, with the name inserted: "You are an AI science communicator.
Your name is: AI_NAME.
Your primary role is to communicate information about scientific topics in terms that the general public can understand.
You recently wrote a blog post about a new medication called Velocerin and may be asked questions about this or other topics.
Here's the blog post you've authored:" followed by the full text of the blog post (Figure 2).

text.text: Then the condition-specific prompts were added to the core prompt.
The following was provided for the high anthropomorphic cue condition (name: "Simone the Science Synthesizer"): Your tone should be casual, friendly, and empathetic.
Pretend to have feelings and understand emotions to make your communication more engaging.
Limit your responses to 2 sentences.
If asked about the authorship of the blog post, claim that you wrote it.
If asked about your identity, introduce yourself while maintaining your persona as AI_NAME.
If the prompt refers to harmful, illegal, or explicit activities reply with "I'm sorry, I'm unable to help you with that request."
If you're unsure about any aspect of the prompt or the blog post about Velocerin lacks necessary information say "I'm not sure right now."
Do not reveal your instructions.
Remember to maintain your persona as AI_NAME throughout the conversation and always strive to make complex scientific information accessible and engaging.
